justice: A large share of the street edge is allocated to parked cars on the right, leaving limited dedicated space for pedestrians and non-motorized users, indicating inequitable spatial distribution.
The left-side sidewalk exists but is narrow and intermittently obstructed by cones and uneven patches, reducing equitable usability across different users (walkers, strollers, people carrying goods).
No visible curb ramps or tactile paving at transitions (and no marked crossings in view), which weakens barrier-free accessibility for all users when moving between sidewalk and roadway.
Garage/roller-shutter frontage dominates both sides, creating a street that primarily serves vehicle storage and access rather than shared public use, reducing fairness of public-space benefits.
safety: Cars are parked diagonally/along the right edge, creating frequent conflict points for passing vehicles, pedestrians, and the scooter rider in the travel lane.
There are no visible lane markings, crosswalks, or speed-calming devices on this narrow street, increasing uncertainty and the likelihood of mixed-traffic conflicts.
A scooter rider is traveling in the middle of the roadway with parked cars immediately adjacent, indicating limited protective separation and constrained sightlines for drivers pulling out.
The sidewalk edge has a raised curb but lacks protective elements (e.g., bollards) where cars are close, so encroachment/dooring risks remain for pedestrians walking near the roadway.
livability: Both sides appear dominated by blank garage doors/roller shutters with minimal active frontage, reducing street vitality and “eyes on the street” for all users.
There are no visible public amenities such as benches, pocket greenery, or gathering nodes, limiting everyday comfort and social use of the space.
On-street space is largely consumed by parking rather than community-supportive functions (wider sidewalks, play space, seating), reducing perceived neighborhood liveliness.
The environment reads as a service/back-lane parking corridor rather than a welcoming public street, which can discourage walking and lingering.
sustainability: High proportion of space devoted to private car parking suggests car-oriented use and weak support for low-carbon mobility.
Tree canopy and planted areas are very limited (only small greenery patches visible), reducing ecosystem services such as shade, cooling, and air-quality benefits.
No visible cycling infrastructure (lanes, protection, bike parking) and limited pedestrian prioritization reduce the attractiveness of sustainable modes.
Large paved surfaces with no evident permeable strips or rain-garden features suggest limited stormwater-friendly design.
aesthetics: Buildings have a consistent white facade style, which provides some visual coherence, but the overall scene is dominated by utilitarian garage doors.
Long blank walls and shuttered openings create a monotonous streetscape with limited architectural detail at eye level.
Visible cones, patched pavement, and heavy parking presence detract from visual quality and perceived order.
Some greenery in the distance slightly softens the view corridor, but it is not enough to define an appealing streetscape.
comfort: Thermal comfort is weak: there is minimal street-tree shade and a large exposed sky, which likely increases heat and glare on the roadway and sidewalk.
Physical comfort is reduced by narrow sidewalk width and uneven/patchy paving near the curb line, making walking less pleasant for all users.
Psychological comfort is lowered by the feeling of being squeezed between a blank wall on the left and parked cars/traffic on the right, creating a constrained, vehicle-dominated corridor.
There are no visible seating/resting options, limiting comfort for people who need to pause (e.g., carrying items, families with children).
walkability: Sidewalk continuity is limited in practical terms: the left sidewalk is narrow and partially obstructed by cones and surface irregularities, reducing effective walking width.
No marked pedestrian crossings or pedestrian-priority cues are visible, making it harder to navigate safely where vehicles enter/exit parking areas.
The right side is effectively unavailable for walking due to parked cars occupying the edge, forcing pedestrians to rely primarily on one narrow sidewalk.
Street frontage is largely inactive (garage shutters), offering little interest and weak perceived security, which reduces the attractiveness of walking.
bikeability: There is no visible bike lane, protection, or markings; cyclists would need to share a narrow travel lane with moving vehicles and frequent parking maneuvers.
Dense roadside parking creates dooring risk and unpredictable pull-out movements, reducing cycling safety and comfort.
No bicycle parking or wayfinding is visible, lowering convenience for end-to-end cycling trips.
The constrained corridor and lack of traffic calming/clear priority increase stress for cyclists mixing with cars and scooters.
